concept.name: Duration hedge
concept.definition: A fixed-income hedging technique that sizes an interest-rate futures (or bond) position so that the dollar sensitivity of the hedge to a small parallel yield change offsets the dollar duration of the portfolio being hedged.
concept.intuition: If your bond portfolio loses $X when yields rise 1 basis point, you short enough futures to gain $X on that same move - matching sensitivities rather than face values.
concept.mechanics: Price changes are approximated by Delta-P = -P * D_P * Delta-y for the portfolio and Delta-F = -F * D_F * Delta-y for the futures contract; setting the two to cancel gives the duration-based hedge ratio N = -(P * D_P) / (F * D_F). The key assumption is that all rates move by the same amount (parallel yield-curve shifts only).
concept.formula: N = -(P * D_P) / (F * D_F), where P and D_P are the portfolio's value and duration and F and D_F the futures contract's price and underlying duration; hedge effectiveness degrades under non-parallel shifts.
concept.failure_modes: Duration is a first-order, parallel-shift approximation: non-parallel curve moves (steepening/flattening), convexity, and cheapest-to-deliver switching in bond futures all create residual risk, and short rates are generally more volatile than long rates in practice.
concept.misconceptions: Matching durations is not matching maturities or notionals: two portfolios with the same face value can have very different interest-rate sensitivity, which is why the hedge ratio uses dollar duration (value times duration) rather than par amounts.
concept.example: A $10 million bond portfolio with duration 8.8 years is hedged with Treasury futures priced at $91,000 with underlying duration 9.2: N = -(10,000,000*8.8)/(91,000*9.2), about -105 contracts short.

citations.source: Jerome Mathis, Derivative Instruments lecture slides, Chapter 6: Interest Rate Futures (based on Hull, Fundamentals of Futures and Options Markets)
